newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian inflation drops to two-year low.
newsitem.headline: Australian inflation drops to two-year low.

text.p: Australia posted its lowest inflation figures for two years on Wednesday and economists said the best was yet to come.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose only 0.3 percent in the September quarter, seeing the annual inflation rate drop to 2.1 percent from 3.1 percent in June and 5.1 percent at the end of last year.
That was its lowest level since the September 1994 quarter and kept alive market hopes of a cut in official interest rates to boost economic growth and reduce unemployment.
"Today's inflation figure was good and the best is yet to come," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.

The key underlying rate of inflation, which removes volatile and seasonal items from the CPI, rose 0.5 percent in the quarter to be 2.4-percent higher over the year, the first time it has been below three percent since the June 1995 quarter.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) targets the underlying rate, aiming to keep it to an average of two to three percent over a run of years.
"A mixture of structural change and flat demand is producing the best inflation numbers in decades," Colonial's Kunnen said.
"We expect underlying inflation to remain below three percent for at least the next 18 months," he said.
The government also welcomed the inflation data, saying it confirmed Australia was a low-inflation economy and would reduce any upward pressure on interest rates.

"The September quarter CPI outcome confirms that the Australian economy has settled into a low inflationary environment, consistent with the Reserve Bank's objective," Treasurer Peter Costello said in a statement.
"This good inflation performance suggests Australia can overcome what has in the past been a traditional speed limit on economic growth," he said.
But despite the unambiguously good result, and continuing weakness in employment, economists said there was not enough evidence for a rate cut to be delivered just yet.
"Today's data would not stand on the way of a rate cut, but it doesn't make one inevitable either," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said.

Instead, the key to a rate cut lay in wages data due on Thursday and on data on enterprise bargaining agreements due in mid-November, following concerns on the pace of wages growth raised by the RBA last week.
Because of that, and as a good inflation result had been expected, reaction to the data by financial markets was muted.

The yield on 10-year bonds rose slightly on the day to 7.54 percent from Tuesday's 7.53 percent. The Australian share index closed 6.9 points weaker at 2346.7, but traders said that was due to market weakness in the United States rather than Wednesday's inflation data.
The Australian dollar was a little firmer at around US$0.7950 in late trading from an early US$0.7940.
"It was probably the least reaction I can remember to a CPI number," Bain and Company senior economist Ivan Colhoun said.

Analysts said they expected Thursday's wages data to show a 1.0-percent increase in the September quarter or a 3.7-percent increase over the year. They said such a result would support calls for a rate cut.

"A good wage number, combined with the low inflation and subdued activity data that we have seen in recent times, would set the platform for another cut in interest rates," said Peter Munckton, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
